full_judgment:
4.12 There is another reason which we may assign here to justify as to why this observation at paragraph 15 of the said reported case is not binding on us. According to our constitutional dispensation, High Court Division is not a sub-ordinate Court of the Appellate Division of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh, it is an integral part of the Supreme Court. Under Article 109 of the Constitution, High Court Division has been declared as supervisory Court having superintendents and control over all courts and Tribunals subordinate to it. Therefore, the lower judiciary of this country has been made subordinate to the High Court Division by specific provision of the Constitution under Article 109. But there is no such provision in the Constitution which says that High Court Division is the subordinate Court of the Appellate Division. The limited jurisdictional power of the Appellate Division over the High Court Division is provided under Article 103 of the Constitution. Sub-Article (1) of Article 103 provides that the Appellate Division shall have jurisdiction to hear and determine appeals from judgments, decrees, orders or sentences of the High Court Division. Sub-Article (2) however, provides that an appeal to the Appellate Division from a judgment, decree, order or sentence of the High Court Division shall lie as of right in three circumstances, namely (a) if High Court Division certifies that the case involves a substational question of law as to the interpretation of the Constitution, (b) the High Court Division has confirmed a sentence of death or sentenced a person to death or to life imprisonment and (c) the High Court Division has imposed punishment on a person for contempt of that division. There may be some other cases wherein the appeal may lie to the Appellate Division as of right when such other cases are provided by an act of Parliament. 

 4.13 Now, the question arises, apart from those cases as mentioned under sub-article (2) of Article 103, how an appeal against judgment, decree, order or sentence of the High Court Division lies to the Appellate Division. The answer is given in sub-article (3) of Article 103 of the Constitution which provides that an appeal to the Appellate Division from a judgment, decree, order or sentence of the High Court Division, in a case to which sub-article (2) does not apply, shall lie only if the Appellate Division grants Leave to Appeal As against this, Article 111 provides that the law declared by the Appellate Division shall be binding on the High Court Division. The further question may now arise as to what is the law declared by the Appellate Division. The examination of the provisions under Article 103 of the Constitution reveal that such 'law' may be declared by the Appellate Division in a case when appeal is admitted by the Appellate Division either as of right under sub-article (2) or by granting leave to such appeals under sub-article (3) of Article 103, and only after disposal of such appeals when the Appellate Division decides a point of law. There is no other way. Under sub-article (2) of Article 103, some cases are automatically appealable to the Appellate Division as of right. But apart from that, appeal may only be admitted to the Appellate Division where the Appellate Division grants leave to such appeal and in granting such leave, the Appellate Division, in leave granting order, specifies on which point of law such leave is granted. After granting of such leave, the leave petition filed by the leave petitioner becomes an appeal before the Appellate Division. Consequently, after admission of appeal as of right, or the leave petitioner becomes an appellant. Therefore, after granting of leave, when the Appellate Division decides a point of law while disposing of such appeal, that becomes law declared by the Appellate Division which is binding on the High Court Division under Article 111. Thus, as stated above, since admittedly leave was not granted by the Appellate Division in the above reported case of SM Mozaminel Hoque, and since the leave petition was filed against HEDAY judgment and decision of the High Court Division which was given in a wrong forum, the observation of the Appellate Division in Paragraph-15 of the said reported case cannot, be regarded as a law declared by the Appellate Division and as such the same is not binding on us in view of Article 111 of the Constitution."
